disease_info: Anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder characterized by persistent restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, and a disturbance in the way one’s body weight or shape is experienced. Self‑evaluation is often excessively influenced by body shape and weight, and individuals frequently lack recognition of the seriousness of their low body weight. Onset is most common in adolescence and young adulthood but can occur across the lifespan, with a course that may be acute or chronic, often associated with medical complications and high relapse risk. It is distinguished from other eating disorders by the combination of significantly low weight, restrictive intake, and the characteristic body image disturbance rather than recurrent binge eating or purging alone.

narrative.personality: Rene is an inquisitive, creative teen who is cooperative yet quietly self‑critical, with a laid‑back attitude toward obligations that contrasts with his intense focus on personal interests like gadgets, gaming, and sketching.
narrative.stressor: Rene’s difficulties began in the last two years of high school, when pressure to improve his grades and figure out a concrete post‑graduation plan left him feeling inadequate compared with more high‑achieving classmates and cousins. As he fell behind on assignments despite being bright and capable with hands‑on projects, he started spending long hours online in gaming and sci‑fi forums where discussions around “optimization,” fitness, and self‑discipline framed strict control over food and body as a way to gain mastery and respect. He gradually channeled his anxiety about exams, his uncertain career path, and feeling disorganized into rigid routines around eating and exercising, telling himself that at least he could be “disciplined” in this one area even if school felt chaotic. Over time, family members and a school counselor became alarmed by how thin he had become and how unconcerned he seemed about it, leading his parents to bring him for psychiatric evaluation when he insisted that his weight was fine and that everyone was overreacting.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My parents keep saying I’m too thin, but I don’t see what the big deal is.”

narrative.personality: Kathia is a methodical, worry‑prone woman who takes pride in meticulous routines, careful record‑keeping, and caring for others through cooking, gardening, and church activities.
narrative.stressor: Kathia’s difficulties emerged gradually after her husband died several years ago, when the shared rituals of cooking and mealtimes that had structured her days suddenly disappeared. Living alone for the first time in decades, she coped with her grief and fears about aging by becoming increasingly preoccupied with maintaining control over her body, worrying about “not becoming a burden” and comparing herself to thin, energetic women she saw in church and old films. She began to alter her recipes, skip portions, and meticulously track her intake in her notebooks, framing it as staying “disciplined” and “healthy,” even as family noticed her clothes hanging loosely and her once‑enjoyed meals turning into highly restricted, ritualized routines. Concerned relatives and a church nurse finally persuaded her to see a psychiatrist when she continued to insist that being smaller was always better and that her dwindling weight was simply proof of her willpower and virtue.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I just want to keep my figure and stay in control so I don’t become a burden to anyone.”

narrative.personality: Charles is a calm, detail‑oriented engineer with a strong sense of responsibility and community service, who values structure and self‑discipline but can overlook his own health needs while focusing on long‑term projects.
narrative.stressor: Charles’s issues developed in the context of a midlife health scare, when routine lab work during a work physical suggested he was at risk for metabolic problems and his physician advised weight loss and lifestyle changes. True to his engineer’s mindset, he approached the recommendation like a project, reading extensively about nutrition and fitness, tracking numbers, and setting increasingly strict targets for himself, initially feeling proud of his rapid progress. Over time, what began as a reasonable health initiative shifted into a rigid, perfectionistic pursuit of ever‑lower weights and tighter control, reinforced by compliments from colleagues and a sense that controlling his body was one domain where he could exert absolute precision amidst the uncertainties of aging and demanding infrastructure projects. His wife and adult children eventually pushed for psychiatric consultation when they noticed he had become extremely thin, fatigued, and irritable around meals, yet he continued to insist that his low weight was simply evidence of his success at “finally getting healthy.”
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve worked hard to get this weight down for my health, and I don’t understand why everyone is suddenly so worried about how thin I am.”
